messages.subject: Improving speed for computation on a huge array
messages.subject_clean: Improving speed for computation on a huge array
messages.body_plain:
Hi list!

I have a 3D array with only binary data (0s and 1s). I want to do computations at each 1 where I would compute the sum around that point over a certain surface and in multiple directions (vertically and laterally). My code produces what I expect, but is very long, even in parallel (~2 h on 6 cores with my smallest data array). I've given a toy example, but my arrays are usually bigger than 200 * 400 * 1000 (~8e7, with about 20% 1s, so 1.6e6 values from which to compute.

toto <- array(round(runif(200^3)), dim = c(200,200,200))
xyz.air <- which(toto == 1, arr.ind = TRUE)

dims <- dim(toto)

halfPath <- 25

ncores <- detectCores() - 2

splitArray <- mclapply(splitIndices(nrow(xyz.air), ncores), function(idx) {
  lapply(idx, function(j) {
    x <- xyz.air[j,]

    #Produce a sequence over which to get the data
    seqRow <- seq(max(1,(x[1] - halfPath)), min(dims[1], (x[1] + halfPath)) )
    seqCol <- seq(max(1,(x[2] - halfPath)), min(dims[2], (x[2] + halfPath)) )
    seqSlc <- seq(max(1,(x[3] - halfPath)), min(dims[3], (x[3] + halfPath)) )

    #Get the total length of the vector
    dimRow <- length(seqRow)
    dimCol <- length(seqCol)
    dimSlc <- length(seqSlc)

    #Compute the sum in multiple directions divided by the area over which it is computed
    verticalLong <- sum(toto[seqRow , x[2], seqSlc]) / (dimRow * dimSlc)
    verticalWide <- sum(toto[seqRow , seqCol , x[3]]) / (dimRow * dimCol)
    lateralLong  <- sum(toto[x[1] , seqCol , seqSlc]) / (dimCol * dimSlc)
    cube <- sum(toto[seqRow , seqCol , seqSlc]) / (dimRow * dimCol * dimSlc)

    return(matrix(c(x, verticalLong, verticalWide, lateralLong, cube), 1, 4))
  })
}, mc.cores = ncores)

Thank you for any advice on speeding up the code!

Guillaume

messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: Box plot help: categorical variable with proportions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Zach,

If I understand the issue correctly, your response variable (breastfeeding status), is binomial, so you can't really take an average with upper and lower quartiles. Therefore, a boxplot would be inappropriate. If you want a bar plot, it would be pretty simple:

ggplot(bf_only2, aes(x=wk, fill = bf)) + geom_bar()

The default will stack the statuses on top of each other. If you want them side by side you can use:

ggplot(bf_only2, aes(x=wk, fill = bf)) + geom_bar(position = "dodge")

You could also calculate the proportion breast feeding at each week and create a new data frame:

library(plyr)
bf_prop = ddply(bf_only2, .(wk), summarize, prop = length(infant[which(bf=="EBF")])/length(infant))

I would actually make a line graph with proportion over time:
 ggplot(bf_prop, aes(x=wk, y=prop)) + geom_line() + ylim(0,1)

Hope that helps!
Rosie

Hi Zachary,

I think what you want is what is referred to as an “annotation” in ggplot, which is separate from a legend.
... + annotate("text", x = X_LOCATION, y = Y_LOCATION, text="Spearman R = -0.394") + ...

If you want to include values from your statistical test, you can use paste() like so:
results = cor.test(SOMETHINGSOMETHING)
... + annotate("text", , x = X_LOCATION, y = Y_LOCATION, text=paste("P =", results$p.value)) + ...

You may want to wrap the results with round() or signif() to avoid excessive decimal places.
​

messages.body_plain:
You can do this using annotation_custom() to add images to the plot individually via a loop:
library(png) #For reading in the image.  There's a similar package `jpeg`
library(ggplot2)
library(grid)  #For converting the image to something usable in ggplot2
library(dplyr)

fish2 = data.frame(habitat = c("mudflat", "channel", "marsh"), catch = c(3,2,6))
fish2 = fish2 %>%               # This pipeline create multiple points for each value
  group_by(habitat) %>%
  do(data_frame(habitat=.$habitat, catch=1:.$catch)) %>%
  group_by()
img <- readPNG(system.file("img", "Rlogo.png", package="png")) # Read in your fish

g <- rasterGrob(img, interpolate=FALSE)  # Create a grid object from the image.  Setting interpolate=TRUE will smooth it.

ggplot(fish2, aes(habitat, catch)) +   #Set up the plot
  mapply(function(xx, yy, ii) {        #Loop over your data frame
    g$name <- ii                           #  Create an object for each point named for the row number
    annotation_custom(g, xmin=xx-1, xmax=xx+1, ymin=yy-0.3, ymax=yy+0.3)},  #Add the image object, mess with the offsets to set its size and positioning
    as.numeric(fish2$habitat), fish2$catch, seq_len(nrow(fish2)))   # Loop over x value, y vlaue, and row number. Note the need to convert the factor to a number.

messages.subject: Re: Randomized incomplete block designs?
messages.subject_clean: Randomized incomplete block designs?
messages.body_plain:
Without knowing the particulars of your setup, I can say that the sample() function is your friend.

Assuming you will have balanced incomplete blocks (within block, every treatment occurs the same number of times): You can set up your treatments as the "x" and with replace = FALSE, it will randomly assign your treatments to each spot available. Just repeat by looping through your blocks, changing the "x" argument according to the number of available spots in each block (i.e. if you have 2 treatments (A & B), and 4 spots in block 1, sample(rep(c("A","B"), 2), replace = FALSE), if you have 2 spots in block 2, sample(rep(c("A","B"), 1), replace = FALSE)).

Things can get a fair bit messier if you have an unbalanced design. In these cases, it can make sense to use some kind of stratified sampling to ensure every treatment occurs at least once in each block.

As far as analysis of messy designs, my go-to reference is:

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/AOS259.pdf

Hope that helps,

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Upcoming workshops: Advanced Beginner Python (4/4/16), Beginner Git (4/6/16) and Intermediate Git (4/13/16)

1. Advanced Beginner Python - April 4, 2016
Instructor: Titus Brown
Location: 1043 Valley Hall, UC Davis Campus

So you've written some Python code and it works! Now what?

This half day workshop will explore "next steps" in Python
programming -

* reusing code by placing it in importable modules;
* code organization overall;
* handling command line arguments with argparse;
* simple testing strategies and tools, including code coverage;
* using virtualenv to install isolated collections of software on
  shared machines;

Attendees should have some Python experience, but need not be experts.

This workshop will be taught locally at UC Davis and broadcast on
YouTube to those who wish to participate remotely.

For more information, see: http://dib-training.readthedocs.org/en/pub/2016-04-04-adv-beg-python.html

Davis participants register here (only if planning to come to the classroom): https://www.eventbrite.com/e/advanced-beginner-python-half-day-workshop-tickets-24039834793

2. Beginner Git - April 6, 2016
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Davis Location: DSI Space, UC Davis Campus (http://dib-training.readthedocs.org/en/pub/DSI-space-directions.html)

Description: Git and related systems are key for replicability when doing any kind of computational analysis. This introductory workshop will cover creating a repository, recording and viewing changes to files, ignoring files, working with GitHub online, resolving conflicts, open licenses, and where to host work.

This workshop will be taught remotely and broadcast to our classroom
via Google Hangouts on Air. We will have helpers in our local room to
facilitate the lesson. The lesson will also be streamed to YouTube and
saved there for viewing at a later time.

For more information, including VT information: http://dib-training.readthedocs.org/en/pub/2016-04-06-intro-git-br.html

Davis participants register here (only if planning to come to the classroom): https://www.eventbrite.com/e/introductory-git-version-control-your-workflow-tickets-24030735577

3. Intermediate Git - April 13, 2016
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Davis Location: DSI Space, UC Davis Campus (http://dib-training.readthedocs.org/en/pub/DSI-space-directions.html <http://g.readthedocs.org/en/pub/DSI-space-directions.html>)

Description: Git and related systems are key for replicability when doing any kind of computational analysis. Topics covered in this workshop include branching and merging of repositories.

This workshop will be taught remotely and broadcast to our classroom
via Google Hangouts on Air. We will have helpers in our local room to
facilitate the lesson. The lesson will also be streamed to YouTube and
saved there for viewing at a later time.

For more information: http://dib-training.readthedocs.org/en/pub/2016-04-13-intermediate-git-br.html
